Publication Title: 2026 International Conference on Information Technology and Computing (ICITCOM)
Abstract: Securing IoT devices against unauthorized remote access is a growing concern, especially as deployments continue to scale globally. SSH brute force attacks remain one of the most persistent threats in this space. In this work, we built and tested a Snort-based inline Network Intrusion Prevention System (NIPS) running on a Raspberry Pi 5, which acted as a mandatory gateway in front of a Raspberry Pi 4 IoT server. The idea was straightforward: force all SSH traffic through a single chokepoint where Snort could inspect and drop packets before they ever reached the target. We ran four scenarios, each with 50 SSH attempts. The first two tested normal trusted and untrusted connections with Snort active; the third served as a no-Snort baseline; and the fourth simulated a brute force attack. On the rule side, we wrote four custom Snort rules - two for IP-based access control (SID 5000001-5000002) and two for brute force detection (SID 5000003-5000004) - paired with a rate_filter directive that escalates rule actions to drop once the SYN threshold is crossed. Results were encouraging. Untrusted IP blocking hit 100%, and the brute force scenario saw 94% of attempts blocked, with no successful logins in any trial. Average CPU overhead stayed around 3%, and RAM stayed well under $2,800 \text{MB}$ even during the attack scenario. These findings indicate that a mandatory-routing Snort gateway can deliver strong SSH access control on low-cost hardware without imposing a resource burden that would rule out deployment on constrained IoT gateways.

Publication Title: 2026 International Conference on Information Technology and Computing (ICITCOM)
Abstract: Volumetric assaults are a serious concern for growing IoT networks. Threats like ICMP and TCP SYN floods can drastically disrupt networks and overburden devices with limited processing capability. Recent research has focused on machine learning, adaptive thresholding, and rule-based intrusion prevention to reduce these risks. However, rule-based algorithms still struggle to find optimal detection thresholds for resource-constrained IoT gateways, while adaptive approaches often demand more processing power. To address this, we implemented a Snort-based Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) on a Raspberry Pi 5 gateway to proactively detect and prevent flood traffic. It uses a detection filter to inspect packets inline and enforces a limit of 10 to 50 packets per 5-second interval. We generated attack traffic and measured performance using ping and hping3, tracking mitigation rates, network delay, packet loss, alert counts, false positives, and hardware strain, particularly CPU and memory usage. Our results show the IPS mitigated these threats without exhausting the Raspberry Pi's resources. The proposed IPS blocked up to 99.6% of ICMP flood traffic, while TCP SYN floods proved harder to process, with mitigation limited to a 26-37% reduction in packet loss. The optimal threshold of 20-30 packets per 5-second interval minimized false positives while maximizing detection accuracy and resource efficiency. These findings demonstrate that a Snort-based IPS can serve as a lightweight, effective security solution for resource-constrained IoT gateways when properly tuned.
